questions.q: Why can't an ML model simply recognize on its own that an age of 200 is impossible?
options: Models automatically reject any numerically implausible value
A model has no built-in knowledge of what's physically or logically plausible — it just treats 200 as another numeric data point unless the data is cleaned first
Impossible values are always removed by the training algorithm automatically
Models can only process values between 0 and 100
questions.explain: A model has no inherent understanding of real-world plausibility; it will treat an age of 200 as valid numeric input unless a human (or a cleaning step) catches and fixes it first.

questions.q: In the lesson's before/after example, why was row 3 removed entirely?
options: It had a missing signup_date
It was an exact duplicate of row 1
Its plan name was in the wrong case
Its monthly_spend was negative
questions.explain: Row 3 had identical values to row 1 across every column — an exact duplicate, likely from an export glitch or double submission — so it was dropped.

options: A value that is always numerically zero
A placeholder like "N/A", "unknown", or 999 that represents missing data but isn't automatically recognized as missing by default
Any value greater than the column's average
A value that only appears in the test set
questions.explain: Disguised missing values look like ordinary data (a string, a suspiciously round number) but actually represent an absence of real information, and need to be explicitly converted to a proper missing-value marker.

questions.q: Why must a fill value (like a column's mean, used to fill missing entries) be learned only from the training split, not the full dataset?
options: Fill values are never allowed in ML pipelines
Computing it from the full dataset (including test rows) leaks information from the test set into training, which is a form of data leakage
The training split always has more rows than the test split
Fill values must always be zero by convention
questions.explain: If a statistic used to clean or fill data is computed using test rows, information from the test set has effectively influenced training — exactly the kind of leakage covered later in this chapter.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of an "inconsistent formatting" problem a cleaning pass should catch?
options: A dataset with exactly 1,000 rows
A duplicate row appearing twice
The same plan name appearing as "Standard", "standard", and "STANDARD" across different rows
A column with no missing values at all
questions.explain: Inconsistent capitalization (or date formats, or stray whitespace) causes what should be identical categories to be treated as different values unless standardized during cleaning.
